prompt.context: A Canadian timber company has hired you. The company processes trees from the forest to make timber products (e.g., plywood, paper). They have been making more profits than their direct competitors and do not understand this phenomenon. You have been hired to find out why.
prompt.question: Why has this Canadian timber company been making extraordinary profits compared to its direct competitors?

clarifying_info.q: Are we also making higher margins than our competitors?
How do our prices compare to those of our competitors?
clarifying_info.a: Timber products are commodity goods, so prices are comparable to those of competitors.

clarifying_info.q: How do our costs compare to those of our competitors?
Are our labor costs the same as competitors?
clarifying_info.a: The hourly rate that workers are paid is comparable throughout the industry. Assume that labor skills are comparable as well.

clarifying_info.q: How do our raw material costs compare?
clarifying_info.a: In Canada, the timber companies own their own natural resources (forests). Assume that the costs of growing and cutting down any given tree are comparable throughout the industry.

clarifying_info.q: How do our transportation costs compare?
clarifying_info.a: There is not much of a transportation difference between the forests, the mills, and the point of sales.

clarifying_info.q: How do our fixed costs / equipment compare?
clarifying_info.a: Assume that we use the same equipment as our competitors.

framework: Apply a profitability framework: Profit = Revenue - Costs
Revenue side: Price x Volume. Since timber is a commodity, check if prices differ from competitors.
Cost side: Break down into variable costs (labor, raw materials, transportation) and fixed costs (equipment, overhead). Benchmark each against competitors.
Value chain analysis: Examine each step from forest to finished product — harvesting, processing/milling, transportation, sales — to identify where the cost or yield advantage arises.
3 C's lens: Company vs. Competitors vs. Customers — focus on what the company does differently at each value chain step.
Synthesize: If prices are equal and per-unit processing costs are equal, the only remaining driver of superior profit is output (yield) per unit of input.

questions.prompt: Given that prices are comparable and all major cost inputs (labor, raw materials, transportation, equipment) are comparable, what could explain the superior profitability?
questions.guidance: The candidate should recognize that if price and per-unit cost are both at parity with competitors, the only lever left is yield — i.e., how much finished product is obtained from each tree. A strong candidate frames this explicitly: Profit per tree = (Price per unit x Units per tree) - Processing cost per tree. Since price and processing cost per tree are equal, more units per tree means higher profit.

math.setup: Profit per tree = Revenue per tree - Cost per tree. Revenue per tree = Price per unit x Yield (units per tree). If price and cost per tree are both equal across competitors, then superior profit can only come from higher yield.
steps: Let P = price per unit (same for all), C = processing cost per tree (same for all), Y_client = yield of client (units per tree), Y_competitor = average competitor yield.
Client profit per tree = P x Y_client - C
Competitor profit per tree = P x Y_competitor - C
Since Y_client > Y_competitor, Client profit per tree > Competitor profit per tree.
math.answer: The client earns higher profit per tree because it gets more finished product units from each tree (higher yield), not because of any difference in price or per-tree processing cost.

questions.prompt: Why does the client have a higher yield per tree?
questions.guidance: The answer is that the client's forests contain thicker (larger) trees on average. Larger trees produce more finished product for the same amount of processing time, which translates into a lower processing cost per unit of output.

recommendation: The client's above-average profits stem from a lower processing cost per unit, driven by a higher yield per tree due to thicker trees in their forests.
This structural advantage — owning forests with larger, more productive trees — is the root cause of their competitive profitability edge.
risks: This advantage may not be sustainable: as older-growth trees are harvested, average tree thickness could decline toward industry parity.
Regulatory or environmental restrictions on harvesting large or old-growth trees could erode the advantage.
Competitors could acquire or develop forests with similarly thick trees over time.
next_steps: Assess how long the current tree stock can sustain the yield advantage (forest inventory analysis).
Evaluate whether the competitive advantage is defensible and for how long.
Explore whether the company can further optimize processing to capture even more value from its larger trees.
Consider whether reforestation practices can maintain or improve tree thickness over future harvest cycles.
